source.title: NeuronMotif: Deciphering cis-regulatory codes by layer-wise demixing of deep neural networks
source.authors: Zheng Wei; Kui Hua; Lei Wei; Shining Ma; Rui Jiang; Xuegong Zhang; Yanda Li; Wing Hong Wong; Xiao-Wo Wang

record.file_problem: The full article is present. Some equations and symbols are garbled in the text extraction, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures motif mixtures in trained convolutional neurons and argues that some apparent mixtures reflect shifted instances of motifs, while other synonymous-motif mixtures are problematic and depend on model design.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results from its own motif-decoupling and diagnostic analyses. The counts of shifted signals are described in the text as expected from pooling sizes. The paper also compares motif-mixture diagnostics and prediction performance across architectures. Motif-matching results and literature cited as external support are not treated as independent findings here.
record.test_reason: A borderline T3 test of V5 in a new setting. In genomic CNNs (Basset, DeepSEA), the study diagnoses neurons that mix 'synonymous' motifs and shows this changes with architecture and regularization, with no performance loss. The construct is only close to polysemanticity: synonymous motifs are functionally replaceable (e.g. reverse complements), not clearly unrelated. Mixture is shown via qualitative consensus-vs-max activation scatter plots, not a reported share. The 'shifted signal' results are one motif at different positions, caused by max-pooling. They are a decoupling step of the authors' method, not evidence on polysemanticity or V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction: the text does not conflict on DD-10. The authors conclude NeuronMotif decouples shifted motif mixtures in max-pooling CNN neurons. Synonymous-motif mixtures act as adversarial-sensitive noise. Deeper networks with small kernels and pooling suppress this, avoid dead neurons and improve prediction; DD-10 needed a first-layer kernel size of 7 to beat DeepSEA.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a genetic-algorithm-based sequence sampler and K-means clustering of feature maps to decouple DNA motif mixtures in max-pooling convolutional networks. It does not reproduce the original visual-neuron examples or their image-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported mixture diagnostics differ by layer: Basset L2 is described as nearly consistent, while Basset L3 shows substantial consensus-versus-maximum activation divergence. Architecture and regularization also affect the reported diagnostics.

fits_no_version.finding: Max-pooling makes a convolutional neuron's preferred inputs a mixture of one motif at K shifted positions. Decoupling by K-means yields consistent motifs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent mixtures in pooled convnet neurons can reflect positional shifts of one feature rather than distinct features.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The study does not quantify a general share of polysemantic neurons. The synonymous-motif diagnostics are described qualitatively, and dead neurons are reported only for DeepSEA in the text. The text gives conflicting descriptions of DD-10 prediction performance, and does not provide numerical AUPRC comparison results there. The method is limited to max-pooling CNNs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct results relevant to the tested versions were left out.

untested.parts: No image classifiers; DNA-sequence CNNs only.
No test of superposition or feature count versus neuron count; the paper's argument concerns kernel coupling.
No test of initialization or noise as causes with sufficient capacity.
No activation-function change (e.g. SoLU). No numeric share of polysemantic neurons; only qualitative scatter diagnostics.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined. Shifted-motif decoupling concerns position, not unrelated features.
No comparison of activation ranges or scoring choices.

missing.what: Result that weaker coupling among previous-layer sub-structures (larger kernel/pooling) increases sensitivity to synonymous-motif noise under the same training
missing.locator: Results, 'DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance'; Methods; Fig. S6

missing.what: DD-10 first-layer kernel-size sweep (3, 5, 7, 9) and its effect on performance
missing.locator: Methods, 'DCNN architecture optimization and deeper DCNN model construction'

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text is the Feb 2021 bioRxiv preprint, not the PNAS version named by the DOI; results may differ. The relevance to polysemanticity is only through 'synonymous motif' mixtures, which the paper defines as functionally similar motifs. A reviewer may judge this a different construct, in which case V5 verdicts should be downgraded to fits_no_version. Methods lists 'DD-5' among the compared models, apparently a typo for DD-10.

versions.untested_parts: Tests DNA-sequence convolutional networks, not neurons in image classifiers such as InceptionV1.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons, or language inputs.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons or by superposition.
Does not test initialization, training noise, or regularization as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.
Tests changes to convolutional architecture and regularization in DNA models; does not test SoLU or modern image convnets, and does not report a general share of polysemantic neurons.
Examines motif mixtures in DNA-sequence convolutional neurons, not the cited canonical visual neurons or whether they detect a shared feature such as pose.
Does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods as determinants of whether a neuron is classified as polysemantic.

rows.subject: Basset
rows.size_stated: 300, 200 and 200 kernels in the three convolutional layers
rows.operation_detail: NeuronMotif decoupled shifted motif signals from layer 2 neurons.
rows.measure: Number and consistency of shifted motif signals
rows.value: 3 shifted signals; the paper reports that adjacent neuron motifs were shifted by 1 bp and highly consistent.
rows.locator: Results, “NeuronMotif successfully decouple the motif mixture”; Fig. 3
rows.note: The paper gives 3 as the number of shifted signals based on the pooling size and reports successful decoupling.
rows.check: Shifted signals are one motif at pooling-determined offsets. The count (3) is set by pooling size, not measured. This describes NeuronMotif's own decoupling, not polysemanticity, and does not bear on V6's canonical neurons.

rows.subject: Basset
rows.size_stated: 300, 200 and 200 kernels in the three convolutional layers
rows.operation_detail: NeuronMotif decoupled shifted motif signals and assessed synonymous-motif diagnostics.
rows.measure: Shifted signals and activation of motif consensus sequences relative to maximum activation
rows.value: 12 shifted signals; many decoupled motifs had negative consensus-sequence activations that strongly deviated from their maximum activation values.
rows.locator: Results, “NeuronMotif successfully decouple the motif mixture” and “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”; Figs. 3–4
rows.note: The paper reports both successful decoupling of shifted signals and substantial synonymous-motif problems in L3.
rows.check: Only the synonymous-motif half is relevant. Many Basset L3 consensus sequences have negative activations, so mixture is present in the original model; this is the baseline for R9. The '12 shifted signals' part is a pooling-derived count from the authors' method. V6 link removed.

rows.subject: DD-10
rows.operation_detail: Compared test-set prediction performance with the original DeepSEA model using AUPRC.
rows.value: The Results section says DD-10 had much better performance; Methods says its prediction performance was similar to DeepSEA.
rows.uncertainty: One-sided t-test is described in Methods; result-level uncertainty not stated.
rows.locator: Results, “DCNN diagnosis and architecture design guidance”; Methods, “DCNN architecture optimization and deeper DCNN model construction”; Fig. 4f
rows.note: The article gives conflicting textual descriptions of the DD-10 versus DeepSEA performance comparison; no numerical AUPRC values are included in the text.
rows.check: The text does not conflict. Methods says DD-10 with first-layer kernel size 3 performed similarly to DeepSEA. Kernel size 7 was then chosen as best, and that final DD-10 is reported 'much better' (Fig. 4f). No AUPRC numbers appear in the text.

source_check.correct: The final DD-10 (first-layer kernel 7) has 'much better prediction performance' than DeepSEA (Fig. 4f, one-sided t-test, no AUPRC numbers). The Methods phrase 'similar to DeepSEA' is about the first DD-10, with kernel 3 in every layer, before the first-layer kernel was tuned to 7.
source_check.problem: The value mixes two DD-10 variants: its Methods 'similar' clause is about the kernel-3 model, not the final DD-10, and the note's 'conflict' is a misreading.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on whether architecture or regularization changes the neuron-level mixture without a performance loss.

tranche.reason: The study gives a new-setting result (genomic CNNs): neuron-level synonymous-motif mixture changes with architecture and regularization, and AUPRC does not drop. It does not argue that a version is wrong, so the reader's T5 is not needed. The construct is borderline.

source_check.notes: The text is the February 2021 bioRxiv preprint ('Deciphering transcriptional cis-regulatory codes from deep neural networks'), not the 2023 PNAS version named in the record, which may differ. The construct is synonymous-motif mixture in DNA CNN neurons, which the authors treat as noise. All evidence is qualitative (figures and text), with no AUPRC numbers.

statements.problem: none for this study. Kernel 3, first layer 7 and pooling 2 are right. 'Visibly suppress' fits the figure-based 'significant suppressed' (Fig. 4b,c, third column). Basset L3 mixture and AUPRC gain by one-sided t-test, with no numbers, are as the text says.

statements.correction: DeepSEA: the authors say strong regularization suppresses synonymous-motif noise at the cost of dead ANs (150 in L2, 120 in L3), with no ablation. DD-10 was built 'without using regularization methods'. With first-layer kernel 3 its performance was similar to DeepSEA. With first-layer kernel 7 it was much better. The kernel-3 model's mixture is not reported.
statements.problem: The 150/120 dead ANs and the kernel-3 DD-10 matching DeepSEA are correct. But DD-10 is an architecture change built without regularization, so it is no regularizer side cost. The kernel-3 model lost no performance, and its mixture level is not reported, so it does not qualify V5.

none for this study. It is listed with no numbers as a CNN study from another group in which an architecture change lowers a neuron-level mixture diagnostic. The text supports this (synonymous-motif problem 'significant suppressed' in BD-10/DD-10).
